title: Prototyping Tools: A Practical Buyer’s Guide
description: A practical guide to evaluating prototyping tools by interaction fidelity, collaboration, user testing, handoff, and product support. Current prices, ratings, and plan limits have not been independently verified.
criteria: Interaction fidelity: test the states, navigation, errors and responsive behavior needed for user research
Design-system fit: reusable components, libraries, variants and how changes propagate to existing screens
User-testing access: realistic prototype sharing, permission settings and mobile-device previews

Migration risk: export formats, existing documents, unsupported products and archive access
Total cost: editing seats, developer or inspector seats, plugins, storage and training

faqs.question: Are the listed prototyping tool prices and editorial ratings verified?
faqs.answer: No. The stored numbers are provisional editorial records, not third-party averages or independently verified prices. Check the current vendor plan, limits, and evidence before making a purchase.

faqs.question: What should a remote design team test before choosing a prototyping tool?
faqs.answer: Have a designer, product reviewer, and developer collaborate on the same representative prototype. Verify share links, guest permissions, comments, revisions, version history, and what works across the devices your team actually uses.

faqs.question: How do we test an interactive prototype with users?
faqs.answer: Set a representative task and observable success criteria. Test navigation, input states, errors, and mobile layouts with participants who reflect the intended users. Note where they hesitate and revise the prototype before committing development resources.

faqs.question: What should we check for developer handoff?
faqs.answer: Confirm that developers can inspect specifications, assets, layout rules, responsive states, and interaction behavior in the current plan. Test how changes are communicated and whether the handoff can be exported or maintained during migration.

faqs.question: Can new teams adopt InVision's prototype service in 2026?
faqs.answer: No. InVision announced the discontinuation of its core design products, including Prototype and DSM, effective December 31, 2024. Keep this entry for historical context only; compare currently supported tools for new projects.

faqs.question: What belongs in a prototyping tool total-cost comparison?
faqs.answer: Include editor seats, view-only access, prototype sharing and testing limits, handoff features, required add-ons, design-system maintenance, training, and migration costs. Verify current pricing and entitlements directly with each vendor.

body:
Prototyping Tools: A Practical Buyer’s Guide

Prototyping tools help teams test an interface or concept before investing in implementation. Compare the fidelity, collaboration, handoff, supported devices, and maintenance needs that matter to your project.

Transparency note: Current prices, ratings, plan limits, and product claims have not been independently verified. Confirm current product availability and terms with vendors before choosing.

Tools to evaluate

Figma

Test interactive prototypes, reusable components, comments, and developer handoff. Verify current editor limits, sharing permissions, and how the prototype maps to the implementation workflow.

Zeplin

Evaluate Zeplin for handoff of specs, assets, annotations, and design-system references. Confirm compatibility with your current design tools and how developers receive changes.

InVision (discontinued; historical reference)

InVision announced that core design products including Prototype and DSM would be discontinued effective December 31, 2024. It is not a current option for a new prototyping workflow. Teams evaluating legacy work should check previously exported files and backups; old project access should not be assumed. Miro acquired Freehand separately in 2023. Primary-source announcement from Miro.

Sketch

Evaluate Sketch for interface design, reusable libraries, and prototype workflows if its platform and collaboration model fit your team. Test file sharing, handoff, and supported devices.

Adobe XD

Verify Adobe XD’s current availability and support status before relying on it for a new workflow. For existing projects, test file access and whether prototypes can be maintained or migrated.

How to evaluate prototypes

  1. Choose a representative user journey and define what the prototype must test.
  2. Test navigation, interactions, error states, and responsive behavior.
  3. Ask representative users to complete tasks and record where they struggle.
  4. Check collaboration, comments, version history, and handoff to development.
  5. Confirm export, file ownership, and migration options.
  6. Include seats, plugins, training, and handoff overhead in total cost.

Methodology

This is a practical evaluation guide, not a verified ranking. Product availability can change, so confirm current support and test the complete design-to-development workflow.

Separate prototyping from handoff and design editing

Tools in a prototyping shortlist may do different jobs: interface creation, interactive user flows, developer handoff or feedback. These are related but not interchangeable. Before buying, identify who must edit a source design, who only needs to comment, and who requires inspectable implementation details. Build one end-to-end example—from reusable components through clickable prototype to developer review—and record the steps that require exports or another tool.

Validate product support before migrating files

For software with a discontinued or uncertain development path, establish current access to existing documents and the formats supported for export. Do not treat a familiar product name as proof that a new team should adopt it. Test asset ownership, version history, account migration and a complete handoff of a representative design before transferring a large library.
